We have a clear colorless solution. Unknown inorganic salt, one cation, one anion. Need to identify. Use systematic tests: flame test for cation, precipitation reactions with reagents, pH maybe for acidic/basic salts.

First, perform flame test (cost 1 mL).

We have unknown inorganic salt, sample 20 mL, clear colorless. Flame test gave yellow flame. Yellow flame typical of sodium (Na+). Could also be potassium gives lilac, calcium orange-red, etc. Yellow is Na+. So cation likely Na+. Could also be some other that gives yellow? Possibly some other like K gives lilac, Li gives crimson, Ba orange, etc. So Na+.

Now need anion. Use reagents to test. We have limited sample volume 20 mL. Use small volumes.

We can test with AgNO3 to precipitate halides: AgCl (white), AgBr (pale yellow), AgI (yellow). Also Ag2SO4? Not typical. Use BaCl2? Actually Ba(NO3)2 to test for sulfate (white precipitate BaSO4). Use Pb(NO3)2 for phosphate (yellow precipitate Pb3(PO4)2) etc. Use HCl acid to test for carbonate (CO2 effervescence). Use H2S acidic to test for metal sulfides (but cation is Na, not relevant). Use (NH4)2CO3 to test for metal carbonates? Not needed.

We suspect anion could be Cl-, Br-, I-, SO4^2-, NO3-, CO3^2-, HCO3-, PO4^3-, etc.

We have sample 20 mL. Use small volumes like 1 mL each test.

First test with AgNO3: mix 1 mL sample + 1 mL AgNO3 0.1M. Observe precipitate color.
